passage:
In the swimming club's waiting lounge, Nandini was three levels deep in her puzzle game when the coach called her group. She didn't hear. Her friend Hafsa was already in the pool.
Mumma walked over, took the tablet and slid it into her bag. "You've missed the warm-up. Go."
"That's not fair! I was about to finish!" Nandini's cheeks burned. She stomped to the changing room and yanked her cap on so hard it pulled her hair.
In the water, the anger slowly dripped away. It wasn't really about fairness. She had just been having fun, and it vanished in one second.
On the drive home she said, "Can we make a plan? Tablet after swimming, not before. And you give me a five-minute warning?"
Mumma raised an eyebrow, then smiled. "Deal. That's better than me grabbing it."

qa.q: What did Nandini miss because she was playing?
qa.a: The warm-up.

qa.q: What was Nandini really feeling underneath her anger?
qa.a: On top she felt cheated and furious, but underneath she was upset at losing her fun so suddenly.

qa.q: What plan did Nandini suggest, and why is it better than sneaking the tablet?
qa.a: Tablet after swimming, with a five-minute warning; it is agreed openly, so nobody grabs or hides anything.

qa.q: How might Mumma have seen the moment she took the tablet?
qa.a: She was probably frustrated that Nandini had missed the warm-up and acted quickly to get her into the pool.

grounding: A girl is furious when her mother takes the tablet, realises she is upset at losing her fun, and proposes an agreed schedule.

passage:
Thursday: At nine sharp, Papa unplugged the tablet in the middle of a game. "Bedtime." Jagdish threw his pillow. "You're so mean! You always ruin everything!" He lay awake fuming, feeling robbed.
Saturday: At Tanvir's flat, Tanvir whispered, "Play on my phone. Your papa won't know." They hid behind the sofa. But every time a door opened, Jagdish jumped. The game wasn't even fun. He handed the phone back after ten minutes.
Monday: After dinner Jagdish sat beside Papa with a notebook. "What if I get one hour after homework, two on Sundays, and you don't pull the plug mid-level? I'll stop at the end of a level myself."
Papa read the page twice. "Let's try it for a week." They both signed it.

qa.q: At what time did Papa unplug the tablet?
qa.a: At nine sharp.

qa.q: How did Jagdish feel lying awake on Thursday night?
qa.a: Furious and robbed, as if Papa had ruined everything.

qa.q: Why did negotiating work better than sneaking for Jagdish?
qa.a: Sneaking at Tanvir's made him jumpy and wasn't even fun, while the written plan gave him screen time openly with Papa's agreement.

qa.q: How might Papa see Jagdish's notebook plan?
qa.a: He takes it seriously, reading it twice, and is willing to try because Jagdish came to him calmly.

grounding: A boy furious at his father for taking the tablet finds sneaking screens joyless and negotiates a fixed schedule instead.

passage:
The school bus came at 6:45, and Zeenat had been awake past eleven watching dance videos under her blanket. At breakfast she yawned into her paratha. Her little brother Naveen giggled. "Your eyes look like a panda's."
Ammi didn't laugh. She touched Zeenat's cheek and looked at the phone on the table. "You look so tired, jaan. I'm worried. This is the third morning like this."
Zeenat almost snapped that everyone watched videos at night. But Ammi's voice wasn't angry. It was soft and worried.
"I know," she mumbled. "I keep saying one more."
"Then let's decide together. Where should the phone sleep?"
Zeenat thought. "In the kitchen. From nine."
That night the phone charged beside the rice tin, and Zeenat was asleep before ten.

qa.q: Where did the phone charge that night?
qa.a: Beside the rice tin in the kitchen.

qa.q: Why did Zeenat stop herself from snapping at Ammi?
qa.a: She noticed Ammi's voice was soft and worried, not angry, so she felt cared for rather than attacked.

qa.q: How did Zeenat and Ammi set the limit?
qa.a: They decided together that the phone would sleep in the kitchen from nine.

qa.q: How does Ammi see Zeenat's tiredness?
qa.a: As a worry, not a crime; she has noticed three tired mornings and wants to help, not scold.

grounding: A girl whose mother is worried about her tired eyes and screen habit listens and sets a limit together with her.

passage:
In their Chandigarh flat, Tarun had been on the tablet since coming home from school. He rubbed his eyes for the fifth time and winced. "Headache again."
Mummy stood in the doorway, looking from his face to the glowing screen. She said nothing for a while.
"Why are you staring? You're always watching me," Tarun grumbled.
She sat on the bed. "Because this is the third headache this week, and you haven't cycled with Jasleen in ages. I'm not angry, beta. I'm worried. If the headaches keep coming, we'll see the doctor."
Tarun looked at the screen, then at her creased forehead.
"Okay," he said slowly. "What if I set a timer for forty-five minutes and then go down?"
"And I'll come and watch you two race," Mummy said. At five, he knocked on Jasleen's door with his helmet on.

qa.q: Which headache of the week was this for Tarun?
qa.a: The third headache this week.

qa.q: Why did Tarun grumble that Mummy was always watching him?
qa.a: He felt defensive and a bit annoyed, thinking she was checking up on him.

qa.q: What limit did Tarun suggest?
qa.a: A forty-five-minute timer and then going down to cycle with Jasleen.

qa.q: How does Mummy see Tarun's screen habit?
qa.a: She is worried about his headaches and the cycling he has stopped; she is not angry.

grounding: A boy who feels watched realises his mother's stare over his screen habit is worry, listens and sets a limit with her.

passage:
Sunday afternoon in their Chennai flat was long and hot. Harish had finished his homework, the cricket match was rained off, and he did what he always did: grabbed Amma's old phone and scrolled. Funny cats. A man slicing soap. More cats. After twenty minutes he couldn't remember a single video.
Then the phone died. Harish groaned and lay on the floor staring at the fan. Nothing to do. Nothing at all.
His little brother Chinmay dragged in an empty shoe box. "What can we make?"
Harish looked at the box, then at the cardboard tubes in the recycling bag. "A marble run!"
By dinner, a wobbly tower of tubes ran from the sofa to the door. Harish hadn't thought about the phone once, and he was already planning a second level.

qa.q: What did Harish and Chinmay build?
qa.a: A marble run of tubes from the sofa to the door.

qa.q: How did Harish feel after twenty minutes of scrolling?
qa.a: Empty and still bored; he could not remember a single video.

qa.q: What could Harish try the next time boredom hits?
qa.a: Sit with the boring moment and look around for something to make, like the marble run, before grabbing the phone.

qa.q: How might Chinmay see the afternoon?
qa.a: As a fun adventure with his big brother, since his shoe box started the whole project.

grounding: A bored boy's habit of scrolling is broken when the phone dies, and boredom turns into a building idea.

passage:
Gopika's cousin Tanuja was reading on the floor when Gopika burst in.
"Tanu, I'm SO bored. Where's the tablet?"
"Charging. Mummy said not till four."
"But what do I do till four? There's nothing."
"Be bored, then."
"That's not a thing!"
"It is. Lie down with me. Ten minutes, no talking."
Gopika flopped down, sighing. The ceiling had a crack shaped like a river. A lizard walked across it.
"Tanu... what if that lizard was a king, and the crack was his river?"
"And the cobweb is his palace!"
"I'm drawing it." Gopika grabbed her sketchbook.
At four Mummy called, "Tablet's charged!"
"Later!" both girls shouted, busy drawing the lizard king's army of ants.

qa.q: What shape was the crack in the ceiling?
qa.a: Like a river.

qa.q: How did Gopika feel before lying on the floor?
qa.a: Very bored and restless, sure there was nothing to do.

qa.q: What did Tanuja's "be bored" idea show?
qa.a: That staying with boredom for a while can spark new ideas, like the lizard king drawing.

qa.q: How might Mummy see the girls shouting "Later!" at four?
qa.a: She would probably be surprised and pleased that they were too busy drawing to want the tablet.

grounding: A bored girl reaching for a screen is nudged to stay bored for a while and finds a new drawing idea.

passage:
Wednesday
Big fight with Amit over the remote today. I wanted the cricket highlights, he wanted his cartoon. He grabbed, I grabbed, the back of the remote flew off and the batteries rolled under the sofa. We were both shouting when Mummy walked in. Worst part: my friend Yusuf was visiting and just sat there staring at the floor. So embarrassing.
Mummy didn't shout. She put her phone timer on the table. "Twenty minutes each. Toss for who goes first." Amit won the toss. I sulked for five minutes, but then his cartoon was actually funny, and Yusuf laughed, and I laughed too.
My turn came exactly when the timer rang. No shouting needed. Might ask for the timer every day.
Sumit

qa.q: What happened to the remote during the fight?
qa.a: The back flew off and the batteries rolled under the sofa.

qa.q: How did Sumit feel with Yusuf watching the fight?
qa.a: Embarrassed, especially because Yusuf just sat staring at the floor.

qa.q: Why did the timer work better than grabbing?
qa.a: Each got a fair twenty minutes and a toss decided who went first, so nobody needed to shout.

qa.q: How might Amit have seen the fight?
qa.a: Amit wanted his cartoon just as much and probably felt grabbed from too; the timer gave him a fair turn.

grounding: A child fighting a brother over the TV remote finds that a timer and a parent's decision are fairer than shouting and grabbing.

passage:
In their village near Karnal, the power came back at seven and the TV flickered on. Mohit wanted the wrestling. His younger brother Pranav wanted the animal show. Both lunged for the remote at once.
"I had it first!"
"You always have it first!"
Pranav's elbow knocked the steel glass off the charpai, and water spread across the floor. The shouting brought Baba in from the cattle shed.
Mohit expected a scolding. Instead Baba sat down. "One TV, two boys. What's fair?"
Mohit mumbled, "Half and half?"
"And who goes first?"
Pranav held up a coin. Mohit called heads and lost. He watched the lions with his arms folded, but by the end he was asking questions about the cubs. Then the wrestling came on, and Pranav cheered louder than him.

qa.q: When did the power come back?
qa.a: At seven.

qa.q: What was Mohit feeling when Baba came in?
qa.a: He felt nervous, expecting a scolding.

qa.q: How did Baba help the brothers settle it?
qa.a: He asked them what was fair, so they agreed on half and half and tossed a coin for who went first.

qa.q: How might Pranav have felt watching the wrestling?
qa.a: He seemed happy and relieved the fight was over, cheering even louder than Mohit.

grounding: Two brothers fighting over the TV remote settle it fairly by taking turns once a parent helps them decide.

passage:
In the hostel common room, evening free hour meant one thing now: six boys on their phones in a silent row, playing the same online battle game. Saurabh sat with them. If he didn't, he was alone.
After an hour his eyes stung, and he felt cranky and strangely flat. He had barely spoken a word to anyone.
Through the window he saw Reena from the girls' block setting out the rounders bats on the field.
Saurabh stood up. "Who's coming for rounders? Reena's team needs players."
Nobody looked up. Then Dev lowered his phone. "Okay. One game."
One game turned into four. Saurabh walked back flushed and laughing. Tomorrow, he decided, he would ask again, and notice how he felt after each.

qa.q: What was Reena setting out on the field?
qa.a: The rounders bats.

qa.q: How did Saurabh feel after an hour of playing in the common room?
qa.a: Cranky and flat, with stinging eyes, even though he was sitting with friends.

qa.q: What did Saurabh try, and what could he keep doing?
qa.a: He invited the others to rounders; he can keep inviting them and notice how he feels after screens compared with play.

qa.q: How might Dev have felt after the four games?
qa.a: Dev was probably glad he lowered his phone, since one game turned into four.

grounding: A boy who feels lonely unless he joins his friends' online games invites them outside and notices how long screen time leaves him feeling.

passage:
Saturday: At Charu's house, Charu and two other friends played the same online game, headphones on, all afternoon. Sabina sat beside them with her own tablet. By evening her head felt heavy, and she realised nobody had actually talked to her.
Monday: After school Sabina texted Charu, "Skipping on my terrace? I have the long rope 😊". Charu wrote back, "Maybe, after my match." She never came. Sabina skipped alone, counting out loud, and felt left behind.
Wednesday: Sabina asked again, this time in person. "Just half an hour. I miss you." Charu looked surprised, then pulled off her headphones. On the terrace they reached two hundred skips together, gasping with laughter. Walking home, Sabina noticed her head felt light, not heavy.

qa.q: How many skips did the girls reach together?
qa.a: Two hundred.

qa.q: How did Sabina feel on Monday when Charu never came?
qa.a: Lonely and left behind.

qa.q: What did Sabina do differently on Wednesday that worked?
qa.a: She asked in person and said she missed Charu, instead of only texting.

qa.q: How might Charu have seen Sabina's "I miss you"?
qa.a: Charu was surprised, perhaps not knowing Sabina felt left out, and it made her take off her headphones.

grounding: A girl whose friend only wants to play online feels lonely, invites her to play outside and notices how she feels after screens.

passage:
Friday: A video Irawati was watching ended, and the next one started on its own. It was a grown-up video with people shouting and hurting each other. She knew she should close it, but she kept watching for a minute. Then she slammed the tablet shut, cheeks burning, and told no one.
Saturday: The pictures kept coming back at bedtime. She hid the tablet under her cupboard and snapped at her cousin Yamini for no reason.
Sunday: While Mummy was folding clothes, Irawati whispered, "I saw something bad on the tablet. I'm sorry." Mummy stopped folding and sat beside her. "Thank you for telling me. You're not in trouble. Tell me what you saw." Irawati told her. Mummy explained it gently, and that evening they set up the child settings together. Irawati slept without the pictures that night.

qa.q: How did the grown-up video start playing?
qa.a: The next video started on its own after the one Irawati was watching ended.

qa.q: What did Irawati's snapping at Yamini suggest?
qa.a: She felt ashamed and upset about the secret, and it came out as crossness.

qa.q: What did Mummy do that helped Irawati feel safe again?
qa.a: She thanked her, said she was not in trouble, listened, explained gently and set up child settings together that evening.

qa.q: How might Yamini have felt when Irawati snapped at her?
qa.a: Yamini was probably confused and a bit hurt, not knowing Irawati was carrying a secret.

grounding: A girl embarrassed after watching something she should not have tells a trusted adult, who explains it and helps her feel safe without punishing her.

passage: Keerthana, you've been hiding the phone under your pillow and not looking at me. Let me tell you something first. When your Vishal Mama was about ten, my friend's older brother put on a video at their house, a grown-up film with things I knew I shouldn't see. I watched anyway, because I was curious. Afterwards I felt sick and ashamed for days. I couldn't even eat my Amma's dosa. Finally I told my father. I thought he would shout. He only said, "Being curious is normal. Thank you for telling me," and he talked with me about what I'd seen until I stopped feeling scared. So, kanna, did you see something like that? ... Okay. Thank you for telling me. You are not in trouble at all. Come, we'll tell your Amma together, right now.

qa.q: Whom did young Vishal finally tell?
qa.a: His father.

qa.q: How did young Vishal feel in the days after the film?
qa.a: Sick and ashamed; he could not even eat his Amma's dosa.

qa.q: What was the turning point in Mama's story?
qa.a: Telling his father, who said curiosity is normal and talked with him until he stopped feeling scared.

qa.q: How might Vishal's father have felt when his son told him?
qa.a: Probably concerned but calm, and glad his son trusted him enough to tell.

grounding: An uncle recalls feeling ashamed after watching something he should not have and how telling a parent helped, then responds the same way to the child listening.

passage:
In the clinic waiting room, Pola sat between Tenzin and Aditi, waiting for his eye check-up. Both children were bent over their phones. Twenty minutes passed.
Pola sighed and spoke to no one in particular. "When I was young, grandchildren sat at their grandfather's feet. Now they sit next to him and are somewhere else."
Tenzin's thumb stopped. His ears went warm. He looked at Pola's hands, folded on his walking stick, and felt a lump of guilt.
He slid the phone into his pocket and nudged Aditi, who did the same.
"Pola, tell us about crossing the mountains again? The part with the yak."
Pola's face creased into a smile. By the time the nurse called his name, the yak story had grown three new bits, and Aditi was holding his hand.

qa.q: Why were they waiting at the clinic?
qa.a: For Pola's eye check-up.

qa.q: What did Tenzin feel when Pola sighed?
qa.a: He felt guilty; his ears went warm as he looked at Pola's folded hands.

qa.q: What small step turned the wait around?
qa.a: Putting the phones away and asking Pola for the yak story.

qa.q: How did Pola feel before and after the phones were put away?
qa.a: At first he felt lonely and disappointed, then happy, smiling and adding new bits to his story.

grounding: A boy feels guilty when his grandfather says children only look at phones, puts the phone away and asks for a story.

passage:
Sunday: At dinner, Vaibhav and his sister Rekha scrolled under the table while Dadaji talked about his old bicycle shop. Halfway through, Dadaji stopped. "Nobody hears me any more. Only phones." He went to bed early. Vaibhav's dal went cold on his plate. He felt terrible.
Monday: After school Vaibhav put a paper sign on the chai table: PHONE-FREE CHAI, 5 O'CLOCK. Rekha rolled her eyes but left her phone in the bedroom. Dadaji looked at the sign for a long time, then told them how he had fixed forty punctures in one monsoon day.
The next Sunday: At five, Dadaji was already waiting with a dusty photo album. "Today," he announced, "the story of your Dadi and the stolen mango." Vaibhav laughed so hard he snorted chai.

qa.q: What did the paper sign on the chai table say?
qa.a: PHONE-FREE CHAI, 5 O'CLOCK.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav feel when Dadaji went to bed early?
qa.a: He felt terrible and guilty; his dal went cold.

qa.q: How did Vaibhav turn his guilt into action?
qa.a: He set up a phone-free chai time at five o'clock, which gave Dadaji people to listen.

qa.q: How did Dadaji's feelings change by the next Sunday?
qa.a: From hurt and disappointed at being ignored to eager, waiting early with the photo album.

grounding: A boy feels guilty when his grandfather says the children never talk to him because of phones, and sets up phone-free story time.

passage:
Bhulu had died in his sleep on Tuesday, curled on his old jute mat by the balcony door of their Kolkata flat. Two days later Bidisha still couldn't stop crying. At school she cried in the toilet. At home she cried into his mat, which still smelled of him.
On Thursday evening Ma sat on the floor beside her. "Tell me your favourite Bhulu thing."
"He stole Baba's socks," Bidisha sobbed, and then, surprisingly, laughed.
They found an old shoe box. Into it went his red collar, a chewed tennis ball and a photo of him wearing Baba's sock on his head. Her friend Ayesha came over with a drawing of Bhulu with wings.
Bidisha tied the box with string and put it on her shelf. The crying came again at bedtime, but softer.

qa.q: What did Bidisha and Ma put into the shoe box?
qa.a: Bhulu's red collar, a chewed tennis ball and a photo of him wearing Baba's sock on his head.

qa.q: What does Bidisha crying into the mat suggest?
qa.a: She was full of grief and missed Bhulu terribly; the mat still smelled of him.

qa.q: What helped Bidisha begin to say goodbye?
qa.a: Sharing a favourite memory with Ma and making a memory box together.

qa.q: How might Ayesha have wanted to help with her drawing?
qa.a: She wanted to comfort Bidisha and show she cared about Bhulu too.

grounding: A girl grieving her dog cries, talks about him and makes a small memory box as a way of saying goodbye.

passage:
"Mumma, I keep hearing Moti's bell. Then I remember."
"I know, Devika. I keep looking for him at the gate too."
"Is it bad that I can't stop crying?"
"No. Crying means you loved him a lot."
"Gurpreet said I should be over it by now. It's been a week."
"Everyone's sadness has its own speed. What would you like to do for him?"
Devika wiped her nose. "Can we make a box? With his bell and the blue blanket?"
"And a letter from you?"
"And one from Gurpreet. She did cry when I told her, actually."
That evening they sat on the floor with an old biscuit tin. Devika wrote, "Dear Moti, you were the best at catching rotis," and cried again. This time Mumma cried with her.

qa.q: What did Devika want to put in the box?
qa.a: Moti's bell and the blue blanket.

qa.q: What was Devika worried about when she asked if crying was bad?
qa.a: She was worried something was wrong with her because her sadness had not stopped.

qa.q: How did Mumma help Devika with her grief?
qa.a: She said crying shows love, shared her own sadness and helped make a memory box with a letter.

qa.q: How did Mumma feel about Moti's death?
qa.a: She was sad too, still looking for him at the gate and crying with Devika.

grounding: A girl who cannot stop crying for her dog is reassured that crying is healthy and makes a memory box with her mother.

passage:
Rain drummed on the tin roof, and Papa's night shift at the bus depot started in twenty minutes. He was lacing his boots when he found Sahil in the corner, holding the empty cat basket. Chiku had died that afternoon at the vet's.
Sahil tried to wipe his face fast. "I'm fine. Go, you'll be late."
Papa took his boots off again. He sat on the floor and pulled Sahil into his lap, big as he was. "It's okay to cry, beta. I'm sad too. That cat used to sit on my newspaper."
Sahil cried properly then, into Papa's damp shirt. His older brother Darshan brought two cups of tea and sat on the other side.
When Papa finally left, ten minutes late, Sahil felt lighter, as if the sadness were now shared among three.

qa.q: Where did Chiku die?
qa.a: At the vet's, that afternoon.

qa.q: Why did Sahil wipe his face and say "I'm fine"?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed about crying and did not want Papa to be late.

qa.q: What made Papa's comfort so strong, given the time pressure?
qa.a: He took his boots off and stayed, hugging Sahil and sharing his own sadness even though his shift was starting.

qa.q: How might Papa have felt when he saw Sahil holding the empty basket?
qa.a: Sad himself and worried for his son, so he decided being late was worth it.

grounding: A boy grieving his cat is hugged by his father, who says it is okay to cry, and feels less alone.

passage:
In the garden behind their Bandra building, Dad dug a small hole under the hibiscus bush. Francis stood holding the shoebox with Snowball inside, his rabbit of four years. His throat hurt from holding back tears. Boys in his class said crying was for babies.
Dad put down the spade and knelt in front of him. "Come here." He wrapped Francis in a long hug that smelled of soil. "It's okay to cry. I'm crying too, see?"
Francis looked. Dad's eyes were wet. Something in his chest let go, and he sobbed until his shoulders shook.
Jasleen from the second floor came down with a marigold and laid it on the box without a word. They buried Snowball together. Walking back up the stairs, Francis held Dad's hand and felt less alone.

qa.q: Where did they bury Snowball?
qa.a: Under the hibiscus bush in the garden behind their building.

qa.q: Why was Francis holding back tears?
qa.a: He felt embarrassed, because boys in his class said crying was for babies.

qa.q: What in Dad's comfort helped Francis let go?
qa.a: The long hug, hearing that it is okay to cry, and seeing Dad's own wet eyes.

qa.q: How did Dad feel about Snowball's death?
qa.a: He was sad too; his eyes were wet, and he was not ashamed to show it.

grounding: A boy burying his pet rabbit is hugged by his father, who shows his own tears, and learns that sharing sadness makes it lighter.

passage:
Class 5 teacher's note, Tuesday
Chinmay came in quiet today; his dog Tiger died on Sunday. At lunch Ujjwal said loudly, "It's only a dog, yaar. Get a new one." I saw Chinmay's face crumple and his fingers tighten on his tiffin lid.
I was about to step in when Chinmay spoke, very quietly: "He was family to me. I just need some time." Ujjwal looked startled and went red.
After lunch I spoke to Ujjwal privately. He said he hadn't known what to say and blurted the first thing. He apologised to Chinmay before home time.
Chinmay spent the last period drawing Tiger beside Meenal, who lost her cat last year. I have told his parents how his day went.

qa.q: What did Ujjwal say at lunch?
qa.a: "It's only a dog, yaar. Get a new one."

qa.q: What did Chinmay's crumpling face and tight fingers show?
qa.a: He was hurt and stung by the words, because Tiger was family to him.

qa.q: How did Chinmay handle the hurtful comment?
qa.a: He said quietly that Tiger was family and he needed time, then sat with Meenal, who understood loss.

qa.q: Why might Ujjwal have said such a thing?
qa.a: He did not know what to say and blurted the first thing, without meaning to hurt.

grounding: A teacher's note shows a boy stung when a friend dismisses his dog's death, who gently says he needs time and turns to someone who understands.

passage:
Thursday
Nitin came to play today and saw Laddoo's empty bowl still by the door. I told him Laddoo died on Monday. He shrugged and said, "It's only a dog. Just get another one. My uncle's dog had puppies."
It felt like a slap. Laddoo slept on my feet every single night for six years. Nobody can "get another" Laddoo.
I wanted to shout at him. Instead I said, "Laddoo was family. I'm not ready. I need time." Nitin went quiet and fiddled with his cap. Then he said sorry, sort of.
After he left I went to Nani, who loved Laddoo too. We looked at old photos together, and she didn't say anything silly at all.
Alka

qa.q: For how many years had Laddoo slept on Alka's feet?
qa.a: Six years.

qa.q: How did Nitin's words make Alka feel?
qa.a: Stung and hurt, as if slapped, because Laddoo was family.

qa.q: How did Alka respond to Nitin, and where did Alka find comfort?
qa.a: Alka calmly said Laddoo was family and more time was needed, then turned to Nani, who understood.

qa.q: How might Nitin have seen the moment after Alka spoke?
qa.a: He seemed embarrassed, going quiet and fiddling with his cap before half saying sorry.

grounding: A child hurt when a friend dismisses a dead pet tells him gently that time is needed and turns to someone who understands.
